Yesterday we learned that a judge ruled that a lawsuit accusing Apple of violating state privacy laws with the facial recognition feature in its Photos app can proceed, involving damages of $32 billion.

Although the two companies are at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, this case has been conflated with a case involving Meta's use of facial recognition, and the court, in allowing the case to proceed, fundamentally doesn't understand how the feature works...

Allegations against Meta previously

To properly understand the situation, we need to start with a lawsuit that dates back to 2015.

Because facial recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify these people, the company did indeed break the law, and ultimately had to settle with the plaintiffs for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law—the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)—which prohibits companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is completely different

There is a major problem with this accusation: when Apple performs facial recognition in the Photos app, it doesn't collect any biometric data at all. As Apple pointed out in a machine learning research paper published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Furthermore, the iPhone only identifies that "the people in these photos look like the same person"—it has no idea who that person actually is. Only the iPhone user themselves can assign a name to them.

Apple's Photos privacy policy also reflects this.

This lawsuit has been making its way through the court system for six years, and I'm shocked that these allegations—which could be so easily debunked with just a few minutes of fact-checking—can be allowed to proceed.

Courts and legislators should be actively supporting privacy-protective approaches like Apple's, rather than conflating them with the privacy-violating practices of companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are attempting to regulate. The most obvious example is, of course, end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, despite not understanding how it works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in everything. But they can invite experts to provide input, and what I find baffling is that lawsuits and legislative attempts with such obvious fundamental errors can persist for years without anyone pointing out the problems.
